who: Daniel Bischoff, head of growth at Purple from 2015

source: Product Startup Podcast 160, 2023

what: Write about 25 intros; have the performer say all of them on the shoot day; put a few thousand dollars behind each; keep the line that holds and sells. The winner was a question that makes the viewer doubt his own thing.

who: Daniel Bischoff, head of growth at Purple from 2015

who: Daniel Bischoff, head of growth at Purple from 2015

who: Jeff Harmon, co-founder of Harmon Brothers, Orabrush, Angel Studios
record: Orabrush to a $10 million company; The Chosen: $10 million crowdfunded after about a thousand tests
source: Tetragrammaton with Rick Rubin, Jeff Harmon
method: Take a how-to that strangers already watch and end it with your product
what: Find a plain how-to on the trouble with proven views (400,000), make it better and funnier, keep its first seconds (the test with a spoon), and only then show the product.
opening: How to tell if you have bad breath
picture: a man in a white coat with a spoon
held_in: Orabrush 2009; before that, the other channel's film alone on the page raised conversion about 30% (D. Harmon)
when: trouble people secretly search for; unknown cheap product

who: Jeff Harmon, co-founder of Harmon Brothers, Orabrush, Angel Studios
record: Orabrush to a $10 million company; The Chosen: $10 million crowdfunded after about a thousand tests
source: Tetragrammaton with Rick Rubin, Jeff Harmon

why_he_says: Can we hook people to the end better, and cheaper per click, if we change the first five seconds?

who: Jeff Harmon, co-founder of Harmon Brothers, Orabrush, Angel Studios
record: Orabrush to a $10 million company; The Chosen: $10 million crowdfunded after about a thousand tests
source: Tetragrammaton with Rick Rubin, Jeff Harmon

what: Run the finished 20-minute piece itself as a skippable advertisement; hook in five seconds, hold for twenty minutes, and only then the maker asks in person: would you like more?

why_he_says: A little taste of what the product is like.
for_client: Cookery teacher: the whole first lesson as the advertisement, then she asks.

method: Claim joined to proof in the headline
what: 1) Write the promise. 2) Take the strongest proof you own (a profession, a credential, an ingredient, a measured cause). 3) Put both into the same first line so neither stands alone; the promise may never be bigger than the proof. 4) Before testing, choose between two first lines by asking which one carries the more compelling proof.
opening: When Doctors Have Headaches, What Do They Do?
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: Says he beat clients' controls 'usually by wide margins of 25 to 100 percent or more' (Bullet 15); Rodale: 'Against other top creative talent, he has never lost a split-run test in selling any of our books' (quoted by Csaba Borzasi).
held_in: Aspirin free-sample ad (tested by Caples): 'won by a fat and happy 71%' over 'Tension Headache?'; same shape is the current control of Bottom Line Health ('How Doctors Stay Well While Treating Sick People All Day').
when: Over-marketed, sceptical, cold audience; health and any category full of big claims; goal: open and buy.
fails: A bigger promise without proof: it reads as hype and is thrown away.
why_he_says: Prospects cut with two questions, 'is it of interest' and 'is it believable'; without a hint of proof in the headline most will not even read.
for_client: Furniture maker film: first picture a removal man sitting on his own sofa at home; words: 'What do removal men buy for their own house? They see what breaks.'
source: Bencivenga Bullet 7 (c. 2008), also Bullet 3

method: IF easy condition, THEN strong promise
what: 1) Take the big promise. 2) Put before it a condition the viewer must meet, reasonably easy (20 minutes a month, owning X, being able to read this line). 3) State the promise after it, no exclamation marks. 4) Show in the next lines why so small a requirement is enough. A moderately easy condition is more believable than a trivial one.
opening: If you've got 20 minutes a month, I guarantee to work a financial miracle in your life.
picture: photo of the named guru beside the line
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: Says he beat clients' controls 'usually by wide margins of 25 to 100 percent or more' (Bullet 15); Rodale: 'Against other top creative talent, he has never lost a split-run test in selling any of our books' (quoted by Csaba Borzasi).
held_in: Givens newsletter magalog: smashed 'The Millionaire Maker' in a split run and was control for years; the same line, all else equal, then beat the Richard Simmons weight-loss control.
when: Big promises nobody believes; newsletters, courses, health; cold mail.
fails: When the body does not pay off why the easy condition is enough.
why_he_says: The condition 'seems to magically switch off' the Yeah-Sure alarm.
for_client: Dental office post: 'If you have eight minutes before work, you can have the gap in your front teeth closed without drilling.' First picture: a wall clock at 8:02 above the chair.
source: Bencivenga Bullet 3

method: The line that tests the reader himself
what: 1) Write the first line in the skill you sell (shorthand, another language, a wiring colour, a musical note). 2) The prospect solves it in two seconds. 3) The solution itself says the promise, so he has proved to himself that he can do it.
opening: F u cn rd ths msg, u 2 cn dbl yr incm w spdwrtng.
picture: the sentence handwritten across a spiral steno pad, above the straphanger's eye level
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: Says he beat clients' controls 'usually by wide margins of 25 to 100 percent or more' (Bullet 15); Rodale: 'Against other top creative talent, he has never lost a split-run test in selling any of our books' (quoted by Csaba Borzasi).
held_in: Speedwriting course for secretaries, New York subway posters; ran many years; the best IF-THEN use Bencivenga says he ever saw.
when: Courses and skills; captive standing audience; a narrow trade.
fails: not said
why_he_says: The condition is met while reading; the reader feels like a genius.
for_client: Car-diagnosis course: first picture a dashboard with four lit symbols; words: 'If you can name three of these, you can earn from them.'
source: Bencivenga Bullet 3
doubt: He reports another seller's ad; no figure.

method: Reason why inside the first line
what: 1) Write the bland claim. 2) Ask 'because?' and find one physical fact of the product or the sale (an ingredient share, a layer count, a fire). 3) Put it into the same line after 'because'. 4) Test: delete the fact; if the line collapses to a slogan, the fact was the hook.
opening: a better-tasting soft drink because it contains 10-percent fruit juice
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: Says he beat clients' controls 'usually by wide margins of 25 to 100 percent or more' (Bullet 15); Rodale: 'Against other top creative talent, he has never lost a split-run test in selling any of our books' (quoted by Csaba Borzasi).
held_in: Slice: 'quickly captured 7 percent of a $30-billion-a-year soft drink market'; Kleenex towels '50 percent more because they're two layers thick'; 'Fire sale! 50 percent off ... because of our recent fire'.
when: Me-too category products; price cuts; loyal habitual buyers.
fails: 'Half Off Sale!' without its reason slides off.
why_he_says: The fact makes the claim reasonable: "there is a good reason to".
for_client: Bakery window film: 'This bread stays soft until Thursday because the dough rests nineteen hours.' First picture: a dough bowl with a chalked clock time.
source: Bencivenga Bullet 9
doubt: Slice was not his own work; he cites it.

method: Flaw turned into the proof, before the buyer meets it
what: 1) Find the visible flaw or accident (hail marks, crooked seam, small size). 2) Say it first, in the first line or on the card the buyer sees first: 'Notice the ...'. 3) Give the true cause that produced the flaw and the benefit that comes from the same cause.
opening: Notice the hail marks on these apples. These are proof of their growth at a high mountain altitude
picture: card lying on top of the hail-marked apples when the box is opened
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: Says he beat clients' controls 'usually by wide margins of 25 to 100 percent or more' (Bullet 15); Rodale: 'Against other top creative talent, he has never lost a split-run test in selling any of our books' (quoted by Csaba Borzasi).
held_in: Uncle Jim's Mountain Grown Apples: 'fewer money-back requests than ever' that year; still gets orders for 'Hail-marked apples, if available'.
when: Natural or handmade goods with visible variation; existing buyers opening the box.
fails: The reason must be true (Bencivenga praises it for proof and honesty).
why_he_says: Every adversity carries the seed of an equal benefit; the flaw becomes the unique proof.
for_client: Oak-table maker film: first picture a finger stopping on a dark knot; words: 'You will find this knot in your table. It is where the branch was, and it is the hardest spot in the wood.'
source: Bencivenga Bullet 8, telling Don Reynolds Jr., Crackerjack Positioning
doubt: Second-hand story told in a book; no counts.

method: First line that musters only the already motivated
what: 1) Ask who already knows he has this problem or wish. 2) Call exactly those people by the wish, not by the problem statistic: 'To men who want ...', 'To parents of a ...'. 3) Never open by proving that the problem exists. 4) First paragraphs feed the wish that is already burning.
opening: To Men Who Want to Quit Work Someday
picture: smiling man in his sixties in a rowboat, fishing rod in hand, looking at the reader
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: Says he beat clients' controls 'usually by wide margins of 25 to 100 percent or more' (Bullet 15); Rodale: 'Against other top creative talent, he has never lost a split-run test in selling any of our books' (quoted by Csaba Borzasi).
held_in: Caples' retirement ad: 'nearly 3 times as many inquiries as its 25 predecessors had averaged ... volume of sales was larger by 4 times' (quoted from Watkins).
when: Any medium with a mixed crowd; paid space; goal: buy.
fails: 'New Survey Reveals That Only 1 in 12 Will Have Enough Money to Retire': he calls it weak, it educates people into a motivation.
why_he_says: 95% are unmotivated and will not be moved; you can only feed a fire already burning.
for_client: Tutoring studio: first picture a boy closing a maths book; words: 'To parents whose child says he is just bad at maths.'
source: Bencivenga Bullet 29 (2008)
doubt: The proving ad is Caples' (an insurance product; the method is kept, the product not).

method: Throw the small ball first (sale before the sale)
what: 1) Do not open with the product. 2) Open with something free and useful aimed only at the buyer you want (booklet on dust mites, trend report of his town's house prices, a sample half-pound). 3) Title it by the trouble it removes. 4) Come back for the sale a step later.
opening: Good afternoon, madam. Today I bring you a special gift, a free half-pound of our finest coffee. Please accept it with my compliments.
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: Says he beat clients' controls 'usually by wide margins of 25 to 100 percent or more' (Bullet 15); Rodale: 'Against other top creative talent, he has never lost a split-run test in selling any of our books' (quoted by Csaba Borzasi).
held_in: Early 1900s door-to-door coffee canvass told by Hopkins; Bencivenga calls free targeted information the most versatile and economical form in his own work.
when: Cold strangers, dear or considered purchases, services (chiropractor, estate agent, cleaner).
fails: 'Any apparent effort to sell creates corresponding resistance.'
why_he_says: You must sell the chance to sell; the first step must be irresistibly easy.
for_client: Carpet cleaner reel: first picture a lamp held flat to a clean-looking carpet, dust visible; words: 'Free sheet: the six places in a clean house where the dust lives.'
source: Bencivenga Bullet 15

method: Find the hook by the product's own unique strength, then show it as a two-choice test
what: 1) List what only this product does, before thinking about what everybody in the category promises. 2) Choose the strength that answers a want the category ignores. 3) Say it in one line. 4) Stage it as a visible either/or in the first seconds.
opening: Which hand holds the M&Ms?
picture: announcer holds two closed fists to the screen; opens one: melted mess; opens the other: clean candies
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: Says he beat clients' controls 'usually by wide margins of 25 to 100 percent or more' (Bullet 15); Rodale: 'Against other top creative talent, he has never lost a split-run test in selling any of our books' (quoted by Csaba Borzasi).
held_in: M&M's TV ads by Rosser Reeves; Mars made 'some $18 billion a year' later.
when: Everyday product in a sea of same promises.
fails: Focusing only on what the prospect wants gives the same promise as everyone ("rich chocolate taste") and is screened out.
why_he_says: A gifted product is mightier than a gifted pen: the message must be unique before the execution.
for_client: Paint shop: first picture two closed paint tins turned upside down over a white floor; words: 'One of these is ours. Which lid do you trust?'
source: Bencivenga Bullet 20
doubt: Reeves' work told by Bencivenga from memory.

method: Borrow a proven headline by SCAMPER (adapt a winner of another trade)
what: 1) Take a headline that won for decades in another field. 2) Keep its skeleton, change the noun. 3) Fill the body with the concrete things the skeleton promises (for 'mistakes': the actual mistakes). 4) If stuck, run substitute, combine, adapt, modify, put to other use, eliminate, reverse.
opening: Do You Make These Mistakes with Vitamins?
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: Says he beat clients' controls 'usually by wide margins of 25 to 100 percent or more' (Bullet 15); Rodale: 'Against other top creative talent, he has never lost a split-run test in selling any of our books' (quoted by Csaba Borzasi). [control listed in the library; Makepeace confirms Bencivenga's controls]
held_in: Health & Healing newsletter: 'One of the most successful packages I've ever written'; 'Every time I've adapted this headline to a product I wanted to promote, it's given me a breakthrough.'
when: Any product whose users make visible mistakes without it.
fails: Cut-and-paste without thinking: when product or market differs it will not work (Bullet 27). He would not use 90 of Schwab's 100 good headlines today (Bullet 15).
why_he_says: New ideas based on proven winners never run out.
for_client: Garden centre: 'Do you make these mistakes with your lemon tree?' First picture: hand pouring tap water on yellow leaves.
source: Bencivenga Bullet 6

method: Benefit built into the name that is seen first
what: 1) Before writing a line, name the product or shop so that the name alone says the benefit (Gentle Dental, Fresh Coat, Easy Off). 2) Let the name be the first words on screen, sign, subject. 3) A known person may use his own name instead.
opening: Painless Parker
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: Says he beat clients' controls 'usually by wide margins of 25 to 100 percent or more' (Bullet 15); Rodale: 'Against other top creative talent, he has never lost a split-run test in selling any of our books' (quoted by Csaba Borzasi).
held_in: 'Painless' Parker, dentist: some 30 West Coast offices, 70 dentists, 'grossed $3 million per year' in the early 1900s; Quaker Bites '5 million Bites a day'.
when: Services and shops with little advertising money.
fails: The name must be free to use; check first.
why_he_says: The best product names have a benefit built in.
for_client: Physio practice video series named 'Back by Monday': first picture the words on the door, hand opening it.
source: Bencivenga Bullet 17
doubt: Examples of others; Parker's treatment claims were not honest, only the naming carries over.

method: Seven times more facts than needed, then the one nugget opens
what: 1) Walk the factory, back office, best salesman, happiest customers with who/what/where/when/how/why. 2) Keep asking why until a fact surprises you. 3) Collect about seven times what you can use. 4) Open with the fact that outweighs a hundred adjectives.
opening: 14 months researching 18,292 small business opportunities
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: Says he beat clients' controls 'usually by wide margins of 25 to 100 percent or more' (Bullet 15); Rodale: 'Against other top creative talent, he has never lost a split-run test in selling any of our books' (quoted by Csaba Borzasi).
held_in: His own practice (credited to Caples' advice); his 1982 'Shoestring businesses' ad opens its body with the counted figure.
when: any product; especially ones thought boring
fails: Lazy research: 'writer's block' is 'LRS, Lazy Research Syndrome'.
why_he_says: No boring subjects, only boring writers.
for_client: Laundry: first picture a counter clicking; words: 'We have taken 4,116 wine stains out of one tablecloth order book. Two beat us.'
source: Bencivenga Bullet 14 and 27

method: Say less than you could (the understated claim)
what: 1) Write the strongest form of the claim. 2) Weaken the verb to what can truly be known (will -> may, always -> often, best -> one of). 3) Keep every proof in the body at full strength. 4) Test the weak verb against the strong one.
opening: Why the price of silver may rise steeply
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: 'I had the good fortune to never have lost a split run test at Rodale' (interview part 3); controls for Hume, Phillips, KCI, Boardroom.
held_in: Silver ad for a Dan Rosenthal client: 'may rise' outperformed 'will rise' 'maybe by 200%', body copy exactly the same; the ad ran many years.
when: Savvy, sceptical buyers; unknowable future; dear goods.
fails: The stronger verb bombed: it promises something unknowable.
why_he_says: Over-promising is the first permission to blow you off; understatement sucks them in.
for_client: Window fitter film: first picture a hand against a cold pane; words: 'Why your heating bill may be leaving through this frame.'
source: Clayton Makepeace interviews Gary Bencivenga, The Total Package (2008 reprint)
doubt: The proving work sold an investing product; only the method is taken over.

method: Turn the tired promise of the trade on its head so it becomes believable
what: 1) Name the promise everybody in the trade shouts. 2) Reverse its tempting word (quick -> slowly). 3) Make the shouting rivals the enemy in the first lines. 4) Give the sober arithmetic that makes the modest version true.
opening: Get Rich Slowly
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: 'I had the good fortune to never have lost a split run test at Rodale' (interview part 3); controls for Hume, Phillips, KCI, Boardroom.
held_in: Hume Publishing course: 'virtually unbeatable for several years', with a headline the client did not want to test.
when: Categories burned by hype (slimming, money, language courses, skin).
fails: not said
why_he_says: Nobody buys without belief; something believable is most of the battle.
for_client: Language school reel: first picture a fat two-year wall calendar; words: 'Learn Spanish slowly. Ours still speak it ten years later.'
source: Clayton Makepeace interviews Gary Bencivenga, The Total Package (2008 reprint)
doubt: The proving work sold an investing product; only the method is taken over.

method: Name the feeling he already has, and stand on his side of the desk
what: 1) Find the anger or weariness the audience already carries about the whole trade. 2) Open with only that, no benefit (three words are enough). 3) Second line says 'we', not 'you'. 4) Show the villains as pictures (cartoons). 5) Only then the product as the way out.
opening: Lies, Lies, Lies
picture: cartoons: a politician taking the oath with his fingers crossed, a cigar-smoking broker, a taxman as Darth Vader
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: 'I had the good fortune to never have lost a split run test at Rodale' (interview part 3); controls for Hume, Phillips, KCI, Boardroom. [confirmed in the interview by Clayton Makepeace, who calls it the classic of its field]
held_in: Mark Skousen's newsletter package, early 1990s: 'extremely successful and ran for many years'.
when: Audience that has tried everything and is disappointed; crowded market.
fails: not said
why_he_says: With a named enemy 'you come around from your side of the desk to be on the reader's side'.
for_client: Garage film: first picture a fan of five repair bills on a bonnet; words: 'We car owners are tired of "while we were in there".'
source: Clayton Makepeace interviews Gary Bencivenga, The Total Package (2008 reprint)
doubt: The proving work sold an investing product; only the method is taken over.

method: Open with what you believe (credo), not with the offer
what: 1) Ask 'what are we really selling?' until the answer is a person to trust. 2) Write three or four beliefs about the trade that cost you something. 3) Say them flatly as the opening ('I believe ...') in a welcome letter, channel trailer, about film. 4) The offer comes after.
opening: First, I believe the purpose of advertising is to sell, not win awards or applause.
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: 'I had the good fortune to never have lost a split run test at Rodale' (interview part 3); controls for Hume, Phillips, KCI, Boardroom.
held_in: His own e-letter (Bullet 1) and the Skousen package.
when: Services, advisers, clinics, newsletters; selling a relationship.
fails: Bland beliefs everybody shares.
why_he_says: Stand for something and you never stand alone; sell him on me before anything else.
for_client: Dentist film: dentist to camera in an empty chair: 'I believe nobody should be sold a crown on the day he came for a check-up.'
source: Bencivenga Bullet 1; interview part 3

method: Wear the clothes of the page it stands on
what: 1) Take the exact look of the editorial around you (real photo, colour border, page-numbered cover lines, article headline). 2) Remove everything that says advertisement; keep every word. 3) Make it really useful to read. 4) A cartoon or 'cute' cover loses to the real look.
opening: Hottest investment opportunities of the next year
picture: cover made like a newsmagazine: coloured border, real head-and-shoulders photograph, cover lines with page numbers
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: 'I had the good fortune to never have lost a split run test at Rodale' (interview part 3); controls for Hume, Phillips, KCI, Boardroom. [confirmed in the interview by Clayton Makepeace]
held_in: Personal Finance magalog beat Jim Rutz's cartoon-cover magalog; 'giant hit for several years'; cites Ogilvy 500% more readership and Caples 81% more orders for article look.
fails: A cartoon cover (magazines do not look like that). When Time complained the border went blue and it did almost as well.
why_he_says: An ad that looks like an article gets read before it is judged as an ad.
for_client: Estate agent: a feed post set like the town paper's property page (marked as advertisement), headline 'The four streets that sold fastest in March'.
source: Clayton Makepeace interviews Gary Bencivenga, The Total Package (2008 reprint)
doubt: The proving work sold an investing product; only the method is taken over. Ogilvy's 500% is hearsay here. Must carry the ad label.

method: Two swings: one safe opening, one that breaks a rule
what: 1) Version A: stack every proven element (big benefit, proof, curiosity). 2) Version B: same body, offer and bullets, but an opening nobody has used in the trade. 3) Never run B alone; A is the insurance. 4) Roll out the winner.
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: 'I had the good fortune to never have lost a split run test at Rodale' (interview part 3); controls for Hume, Phillips, KCI, Boardroom.
held_in: His practice across 40 years of client tests: most of the time A wins, now and then B is a blockbuster.
when: Every paid launch with money for two panels.
fails: Going into a test with only the original idea.
why_he_says: Two panels virtually double the chance; the odds of the odd one are small, the payoff large.
for_client: Furniture shop: film A opens on before/after of a room; film B opens on the owner sawing his own sofa in half.
source: Clayton Makepeace interviews Gary Bencivenga, The Total Package (2008 reprint)
doubt: shelf none: a way of testing, not a reason to stop.

method: Give first in the subject line, or be deleted unread
what: 1) Assume 25 subjects on one screen and about three survive. 2) Only a subject that promises a real nugget, from a sender who gave nuggets before, survives. 3) Hold back selling for several mails. 4) Then sell.
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: 'I had the good fortune to never have lost a split run test at Rodale' (interview part 3); controls for Hume, Phillips, KCI, Boardroom.
held_in: His own reading and his client e-zines (food and wine newsletter partner).
fails: Senders whose every mail pitches: deleted even when famous.
why_he_says: You must sell the relationship before the product.
for_client: Deli newsletter subject: 'The 40-cent trick that keeps basil alive nine days'.
source: Clayton Makepeace interviews Gary Bencivenga, The Total Package (2008 reprint)

method: Entertainment only if it closes the sale
what: 1) Every odd or funny element in the opening must be a fact or picture of the product's own use. 2) Ask: if the viewer remembers only this second, does he remember the product? 3) If he remembers the joke, throw it away.
opening: I can't believe I ate the whole thing
who: Gary Bencivenga, direct-mail copywriter (ex Ogilvy & Mather; Boardroom, Rodale, KCI)
record: 'I had the good fortune to never have lost a split run test at Rodale' (interview part 3); controls for Hume, Phillips, KCI, Boardroom.
held_in: Counter-example: Alka-Seltzer: very entertaining, 'sales plummeted'; Reeves' 'vampire video'. No pun or joke headlines in his own work since his first copy chief.
fails: Extraneous jokes; clever headlines seeking applause.
why_he_says: Copywriters who show off are like fishermen who reveal the hook.
for_client: Pizza oven: instead of a comic uncle, open on the basil leaf crisping at second three.
source: Clayton Makepeace interviews Gary Bencivenga, The Total Package (2008 reprint)
doubt: The Alka-Seltzer sales claim is his memory; other shelves of the library hold jokes that sold.

method: The neighbour's news: name the local person and state the deal as a newspaper fact
what: 1) Write the sweetest offer first; if there is nothing to say, sweeten it. 2) Begin with who: not the unknown name but the most specific real role ('Local dentist', 'Angry wife', 'Local furniture dealer'). 3) 'says he will ...' + the two strongest parts of the offer, in one plain sentence. 4) Next line answers WHY he would do that.
opening: Local Dentist Says He Will Buy A Free Trip To Vegas And A Year's Worth Of Gas For Anybody Who Decides To Buy His 2-Year-Old Caddy!
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure); took Tova 9 'from $20,000 to over $800,000 per month' (his and Blade Thomas' word).
held_in: Taught example; same shape in his Kacey Fine Furniture ads (Denver): sales up 40% in six weeks on $14 million a year, 10 new employees in two weeks.
when: Local shop or single person nobody knows; a real, unusual deal; mail, paper, local post.
fails: An ordinary offer: no headline will save it.
why_he_says: Specific who = someone real you could phone or visit; what you have to say beats how.
for_client: Furniture shop reel: first picture a woman pulling a chair out of the shop window; words: 'Furniture dealer's wife makes him empty the shop before the holiday.' (only if true)
source: The Gary Halbert Letter, "Get it going"

method: Say what you have to say (the owner's own spoken reason is the headline)
what: 1) Ask the owner: what is the big thing you have to say? 2) Ask 'why is that?' 3) Write down his spoken answer. 4) Print it nearly as he said it, as news with the human cause in front.
opening: She's fed up... Angry Wife Forces Local Businessman To Almost Give Away Everything He's Got In His Store!
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure); took Tova 9 'from $20,000 to over $800,000 per month' (his and Blade Thomas' word).
held_in: His way with clients ("All I did here is say what he had to say"); Kacey Furniture because-ads (bulldozers tearing up the street).
when: Small businesses; sales with a human reason.
fails: Invented reasons: the headline must be true and relevant.
why_he_says: People pay to be helped to say what they have to say.
for_client: Tile shop: first picture a digger at the door; words: 'They are tearing up our street until May. Walk three blocks and the tiles cost you a third less.'
source: The Gary Halbert Letter, "Get it going"

method: First sentence of the body: IF you want X, this is for you / what is in it for him
what: 1) After the headline, first sentence: 'If you would like to know/own/have ..., this is the most interesting message you will ever read.' 2) Second: 'Here is why:' 3) Third: begin a true story of a named person. Never warm up.
opening: If you would like to know how someone can start with a simple idea... and then... generate over $51,000,000 in sales in just one year... this is going to be the most interesting message you will ever read. Here is why:
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure); took Tova 9 'from $20,000 to over $800,000 per month' (his and Blade Thomas' word).
held_in: 'This is a staple opening for me. I use it over and over because it's a reliable winner' (water ad).
when: Any channel after a strong first line; cold readers.
fails: Too many sales messages lose the reader right after the headline because nothing interesting follows.
why_he_says: He must be told what is in it for him if he takes the time.
for_client: Physio: 'If you want to get out of your car without holding the door, give me one minute. Here is why: ...' First picture: a hand gripping a car door frame.
source: The Gary Halbert Letter, 21 Nov 2005 (water ad revealed)

method: Find the secret wish of exactly this audience, one shade finer than the obvious one
what: 1) Read what only that group reads, and books where 200 of them speak. 2) Write the obvious desire (money). 3) Sharpen it one step ('not greed: an edge, to be first'). 4) The first line whispers only that. 5) Choose the place where that group stands undiluted.
opening: WARNING: Do Not Read This Unless You Are Already Rich!
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure); took Tova 9 'from $20,000 to over $800,000 per month' (his and Blade Thomas' word).
held_in: Water ad in Investor's Business Daily; his own one-column $700 ads there 'typical ... to fetch $40,000 to $50,000'.
fails: The same ad in a fat general paper: he bets 700% less profit.
why_he_says: No more of an edge than knowing the hidden desires of the people.
for_client: Wedding florist: not 'beautiful flowers' but 'nobody will have the same table'. First words: 'Do not save this if your cousin is getting married the same summer.'
source: The Gary Halbert Letter, 21 Nov 2005
doubt: The proving ad raised interest in a share issue (investing); the opening line is not taken over as a winner.

method: Make him look in his own house
what: 1) Give a small physical act he can do now in his home (cut a pipe, smell a filter, hold a lamp flat). 2) Say exactly what he will see. 3) That sight is the problem your product ends.
opening: Do you own a house? If so, go down into your basement with a hacksaw and cut off about an inch of one of your water pipes.
picture: inside of a cut water pipe under a strong flashlight
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure); took Tova 9 'from $20,000 to over $800,000 per month' (his and Blade Thomas' word).
held_in: Water ad (Seychelle filter bottle), his most asked-about ad.
when: Hidden dirt, wear, loss: water, mattresses, chimneys, gutters, software bills.
fails: not said
why_he_says: He makes the problem real and everybody's own.
for_client: Mattress cleaner: first picture a hand lifting a sheet, phone torch flat on the mattress; words: 'Turn your light off and hold your phone like this.'
source: The Gary Halbert Letter, 21 Nov 2005
doubt: Part of the body, not the first line; fear must be true.

method: Attach a thing and say at once why it is there (two reasons)
what: 1) Put one small real thing at the top (penny, stamp, sand, feather, coal, card he presses). 2) First sentence: 'As you can see, I have attached ... Why?' 3) Reason one: 'I needed some way to make sure this would catch your attention.' 4) Reason two ties the thing to the product itself. 5) In film: the thing in the hand, close, before the face.
opening: As you can see, I have attached a bright, shiny penny to the top of this letter. Why have I done this? Actually, there are two reasons:
picture: a real coin fixed at the head of the letter
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure); took Tova 9 'from $20,000 to over $800,000 per month' (his and Blade Thomas' word). [dollar letter result printed in the Robert Collier Letter Book, quoted by Halbert]
held_in: Dollar-bill hospital letter (Robert Collier Letter Book): better than 90% response, $270,000 from 175,000; modern retest again 90%+; realtor Don Clifton's $1 survey cheque: 538 back of fewer than 1,500.
when: Mail, unboxing, first film frame; a thing with a true tie to the product.
fails: A grabber without a tie ('A submarine that flies?') makes the reader feel cheated and angry.
why_he_says: It brings 'focused attention, quality attention': he must read to find out what it is.
for_client: Roofer letter and reel: a cracked nail taped to the page; 'This nail is from a roof four doors from you. I am sending it for two reasons.'
source: The Gary Halbert Letter, "Grabbers"

method: Snapshot instead of brochure
what: 1) Leave the printed brochure out. 2) Put in what looks like (and is) an ordinary snapshot: the maker, the special part, the first piece. 3) Say why there is no brochure yet. 4) For film: phone picture of the thing on the workbench before any polished shot.
picture: plain amateur photograph of the person signing or of the part that makes the product work
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure); took Tova 9 'from $20,000 to over $800,000 per month' (his and Blade Thomas' word).
held_in: His own mailings; he promises it 'catapults direct mail response'.
fails: Staged; it must be true that brochures are not printed.
why_he_says: A photo is personal and warm, a brochure cold.
for_client: Knife maker's first post: phone photo of the first blade on a newspaper: 'I have no catalogue yet. This is number one.'
source: The Gary Halbert Letter, "Grabbers"

method: Look like a person, and do not break it in the second after opening
what: 1) Outside: nothing that shouts selling (real stamp, written name, sender's address, no teaser). 2) Inside first sight: one plain letter only. 3) Put order form and brochure in a second closed envelope: 'Please open this as soon as you have read my letter.' 4) For screens: a plain-text mail or a person talking; product card only after the story.
opening: Please Open This Envelope As Soon As You Have Read My Letter. Thanks. GH
picture: plain white envelope, live stamp, typed name, only a return address
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure); took Tova 9 'from $20,000 to over $800,000 per month' (his and Blade Thomas' word).
held_in: Crest letter (one page, 361 words): 7,300,000 buyers; a vitamin-trade mailer reformatted in 45 minutes, nearly the same words: about $96,000 more every month.
when: Mail, e-mail, direct messages; unknown seller.
fails: The 'Oh, yuck!' when glossy graphics fall out; he learned personal look must hold inside too.
why_he_says: Everybody opens the A-pile; never opened is the number one reason for failure.
for_client: Clinic e-mail in plain text from the dentist's own name: 'Mrs Kaya, your X-ray from March is on my desk.' Link only at the end.
source: The Gary Halbert Letter, "Direct mail nerd"
doubt: Hand hiding of the commercial sender would be a false front; use only with a true named sender. Contradicts Denny Hatch's collection of teaser-copy controls.

method: Write as if your head depended on one answer
what: 1) Imagine you may send one opening to one stranger and lose your head if he does not answer. 2) Strike everything you would not dare (bulk label, clever teaser, logo, brochure). 3) Keep only what one person would do to reach one person.
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure); took Tova 9 'from $20,000 to over $800,000 per month' (his and Blade Thomas' word).
held_in: Led to the crest letter after three years of failed, textbook mailings.
when: Any opening when rules of the trade have failed.
fails: Following the trade books: every textbook mailing failed.
why_he_says: It forces the true question: would I open this?
for_client: Before shooting, the plumber answers: if one viewer had to call you today or you close, what would you show first? (the burst pipe he fixed this morning).
source: The Gary Halbert Letter, "Direct mail nerd"
doubt: shelf none: a way of finding, not a reason to stop.

method: His own family name is the subject of the message
what: 1) Take a fact about the reader's own name, street, town. 2) First sentence states the fact as a discovery, not an offer. 3) Second: how we came to find it while doing something for people with the same name. 4) Then the modest thing for sale.
opening: Did you know that your family name was recorded with a coat-of-arms in ancient heraldic archives more than seven centuries ago?
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure); took Tova 9 'from $20,000 to over $800,000 per month' (his and Blade Thomas' word).
held_in: Halbert's Inc. letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers; offset print per surname brought in $21,900,000.
when: Personal goods, local services; list known.
fails: 'Some of the names pulled like crazy and some names didn't work at all.'
why_he_says: Call him by name; the fake-computer-letter effect without the cost.
for_client: House painter: 'Your house on Elm Street was green in 1962. We found the old tin in the cellar of number 14.'
source: The Gary Halbert Letter, "AIDA" (letter openings)

method: Open with a story-start, not a pitch: an unlikely person, a place, a sentence broken by "Here is why"
what: 1) First line names a person in an unlikely position ('There's a guy in California who was very wealthy and very bored'; 'I am not a doctor'). 2) One odd concrete fact about him. 3) What he did because of it. 4) The thing he found is the product. Write ten such starts and choose.
opening: My name is Betty Adams and, the first thing you should know about me is... I am not a doctor.
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure); took Tova 9 'from $20,000 to over $800,000 per month' (his and Blade Thomas' word).
held_in: List of openings he used in his letters and ads (Tova, Seychelle, crest, weight-loss).
when: After any headline; films with a person.
fails: "The most-often missing ingredient in a sales message is the sales message doesn't tell an interesting story."
why_he_says: Getting started is the hardest; story keeps interest after the headline.
for_client: Orthopaedic insole maker: 'I sold shoes for 22 years and my own feet hurt every day of it.' First picture: him barefoot among shoe boxes.
source: The Gary Halbert Letter, "AIDA"
doubt: Several of the sample letters make hard health/tax claims: shape only.

method: Odd true fact, then "I mention this because"
what: 1) Keep a file of strange true facts (118 ridges on a dime). 2) Open with one, flat. 3) Second sentence turns it: 'I mention this because ...' / 'That reminds me ...' onto the exact problem your product ends. 4) The turn must be valid, not cute.
opening: On average, a Twinkie will explode in a microwave in 45 seconds.
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure); took Tova 9 'from $20,000 to over $800,000 per month' (his and Blade Thomas' word).
held_in: His own letters and newsletters; shown on twelve facts.
when: Dull products; e-mail, letters, short films.
fails: "the idea is not to come up with something cute but something that is valid and will lead to a sale".
why_he_says: A fact earns interest after the headline and carries him into the message.
for_client: Call-centre software: 'A popcorn kernel bursts in under two minutes. Your callers hang up sooner.' First picture: one kernel in a pan.
source: The Gary Halbert Letter, "Interesting facts" (Dec 2003)
doubt: No result given for any of the twelve samples; the method contradicts his own rule that a grabber must be relevant unless the turn is honest.

method: Bullet twist: take the sober fact from the page and cover its answer
what: 1) Read the product; mark a useful, surprising instruction. 2) Say the gain and the place, hide the how ('What you should do to the lightbulbs in your house that can help you sell it'). 3) Keep it 100% true: twist, never distort. 4) Use the best one alone as a film's first line.
opening: How to sell your home faster by taking it off the market!
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure); took Tova 9 'from $20,000 to over $800,000 per month' (his and Blade Thomas' word).
held_in: His ad for 'Sell Your House Fast'; one bullet hidden in an Entrepreneur ad brought calls for months, 'maybe even a year later'.
when: Information, courses, guides, services with know-how.
fails: A bullet that attracts the wrong people (he regrets the one that pulled most).
why_he_says: Many order because just one bullet appealed.
for_client: Estate agent reel: first picture a hand unscrewing a bulb; words: 'One drop on this, ten minutes before the viewing.'
source: The Gary Halbert Letter, "Do the twist"

method: Nugget notes, star them, then leave the desk: the hook arrives
what: 1) Collect product, rivals' ads, buyers' lists, headline cards. 2) Note every nugget in fragments, no order. 3) Star the good, double-star the better, triple the hot. 4) Stop for a day or two. 5) Deal out old headline cards like playing cards and let one collide with a fact.
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure); took Tova 9 'from $20,000 to over $800,000 per month' (his and Blade Thomas' word).
held_in: His routine; the Kacey free-samples headline is built live this way; clients' furniture sales +40% in six weeks.
fails: Writing before gathering.
why_he_says: The unconscious connects the dots if it has the right dots.
for_client: For a bakery: 40 facts on cards, three stars on 'dough older than the baker', shot first.
source: The Boron Letters, ch. 15 (1984)
doubt: shelf none: way of finding.

method: The sale is decided at the first look, so the first frame must lift
what: 1) Judge the opening without reading it: is it crisp, clean, bright, high contrast, easy? 2) Lead with an uplifting picture (the 'after'), not a depressing one. 3) Show people of the buyer's own sex. 4) Only then judge the words.
picture: bright, clean layout; the happy "after" woman
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure); took Tova 9 'from $20,000 to over $800,000 per month' (his and Blade Thomas' word).
held_in: Before/after ad of Christi Dean: 'almost everybody liked the look of that ad because the after picture ... was so uplifting'.
when: Beauty, home, health; any visual medium.
fails: Cheap, limp, soggy-looking pictures.
why_he_says: People decide in a fraction of a second and then look for reasons.
for_client: Kitchen fitter: first frame the lit finished worktop with bread on it; the old one only at second two.
source: The Boron Letters, ch. 19 (1984)
doubt: Contradicts trouble-first openings in the library; he gives no test.

method: Sales detective: the hook is in the story the owner thinks nobody wants
what: 1) Interview the person who invented or makes it, not the brochure; also the secretaries, salesmen, the wife who hears what people say. 2) Around minute 45 ask: how did you come upon this? 3) When he says 'nobody wants to hear that', say 'I do'. 4) Take that scene into the first line. 5) Show the client's other people the same way; each has one.
opening: Amazing Secret Discovered By One-Legged Golfer Adds 50 Yards to Your Drives, Eliminates Hooks and Slices
picture: a one-legged man in perfect balance on the first tee
who: John Carlton, direct-response copywriter (OHP golf, self-defence, health)
record: One-legged golfer ad: 'ran in the golf magazines for 15 years, and it's still running online'; still paying him royalties in 2026 (his page). [one-legged golfer ad named by Makepeace (AWAI) and Shleyner as a winner; Carlton still shows royalties]
held_in: OHP golf video ad (1990s): 15 years in golf magazines, still online; next hook (a man who left his deathbed and qualified for the U.S. Open) also went to the headline.
when: Any product made or taught by a person; crowded how-to markets.
fails: 'You're not gonna find your story in the company line' (brochure).
why_he_says: Real stories hide because the owner is embarrassed or used to them.
for_client: Cheese maker reel: first picture a blackened kettle; words: 'My grandmother burned this batch in 1961. It is the only one people still ask for.'
source: John Carlton on Copyblogger, A 30-minute copywriting course (2012)

method: Incongruity that bites on the product itself
what: 1) Put two things together that should not go together (one leg + balance sport). 2) The mismatch must touch exactly the ability the product gives. 3) Test: would the oddity change anything in this trade? If not (one-legged accountant), throw it away. 4) Then add the big promise in the same line.
opening: one-legged golfer
who: John Carlton, direct-response copywriter (OHP golf, self-defence, health)
record: One-legged golfer ad: 'ran in the golf magazines for 15 years, and it's still running online'; still paying him royalties in 2026 (his page). [same ad, as above]
held_in: Golfer ad; copycats with one-legged accountants failed, he says.
fails: 'The one-legged accountant, that's not a hook. It doesn't matter if he has one leg or not.'
why_he_says: 'the incongruous juxtaposition of compelling sales elements'.
for_client: Hearing-aid shop: 'The piano tuner who wears two of these.' First picture: hearing aid beside a tuning fork.
source: John Carlton on Copyblogger (2012)

method: The sensitive fact the client hoped to leave out becomes the headline
what: 1) Keep calling the client back until he is annoyed. 2) Listen for 'I was hoping we wouldn't have to go there'. 3) Verify it. 4) Put that fact, not the features, into the headline.
who: John Carlton, direct-response copywriter (OHP golf, self-defence, health)
record: One-legged golfer ad: 'ran in the golf magazines for 15 years, and it's still running online'; still paying him royalties in 2026 (his page).
held_in: A 20-year client with many million-dollar successes: found after several calls with the product's embarrassing superiority over others; it went into the headline.
when: When features and benefits are listed and nothing bites.
fails: Templates and ripping ads before the hook is found; sometimes there is none.
why_he_says: "A great hook will HIDE from you"; it makes the brain say "Hey, wait a minute".
for_client: Upholsterer: what he hoped not to say: 'We re-stuff sofas that are two years old.' First picture: a new-looking sofa cut open, dust inside.
source: John Carlton, Fishing for Hooks (Oct 2006)
doubt: He names no product and no figure.

method: The nobody who beats the experts
what: 1) Choose an unknown outsider with a startling, provable result. 2) Name his plain origin in the first line ('a skinny kid from Fresno'). 3) Use the audience's distrust of experts ('Why almost all the experts are dead wrong about ...'). 4) Prove by ordinary people's testimony.
opening: How A Skinny Kid From Fresno Accidentally Started Hitting 400-Yard Drives
who: John Carlton, direct-response copywriter (OHP golf, self-defence, health)
record: One-legged golfer ad: 'ran in the golf magazines for 15 years, and it's still running online'; still paying him royalties in 2026 (his page).
held_in: Of 'all the hundred and something golf instruction products I've written copy for, all but ONE featured nobodies'; the one with a timid expert bombed.
when: Markets where buyers were disappointed by experts; unknown seller.
fails: The expert afraid for his reputation: copy too timid, ad bombed. An expert only shortens credibility, he does not sell.
why_he_says: A nobody has to share it all; it is a secret between two people.
for_client: Window cleaner course: 'A school caretaker's streak-free trick that hotel crews now copy.' First picture: an old squeegee wrapped in a sock.
source: John Carlton, John Does His Job (Apr 2005)

method: Opening line as a shove: If you have ever wanted X, then
what: 1) Headline stops; opening line must push. 2) Use 'If you've ever wanted to ..., then this is going to be the most exciting message you ever read.' 3) No 'in a moment', no childhood, no joke. 4) Tease what you have; do not let the air out.
opening: If you've ever wanted to ... then this is gonna be the most exciting message you ever read.
who: John Carlton, direct-response copywriter (OHP golf, self-defence, health)
record: One-legged golfer ad: 'ran in the golf magazines for 15 years, and it's still running online'; still paying him royalties in 2026 (his page).
held_in: His fall-back opening; 'often perform better than original prose anyway'.
when: When nothing original comes; letters, pages, videos after the hook.
fails: "Cute don't sell. Selling sells."
why_he_says: The opening sits the reader at the top of the slide and shoves.
for_client: Curtain studio video after the hook: 'If your bedroom is light at five in the morning, stay for twenty seconds.'
source: John Carlton, John Does His Job (Apr 2005)

method: Fifty wild headlines, then walk the outrageous one back
what: 1) Write bullets first until you know the product. 2) Write the plain how-to headline. 3) Write 50 to 100 more, past good taste, for nobody's eyes. 4) Take the wildest that has life and walk it back step by step until it is true and printable. 5) It ends more outrageous than the how-to, less than the jail one.
who: John Carlton, direct-response copywriter (OHP golf, self-defence, health)
record: One-legged golfer ad: 'ran in the golf magazines for 15 years, and it's still running online'; still paying him royalties in 2026 (his page).
held_in: His way of working on controls.
fails: Often the first simple how-to is what remains: keep it as the measure.
why_he_says: Beyond what you know works lies the one that will really work.
for_client: Pest control: from 'What lived in the school kitchen' (unprintable) back to 'We moved one fridge. Count what is behind it.'
source: John Carlton on Copyblogger (2012)
doubt: shelf none: way of working; walked-back line must still be true.

method: Three-line story, then "And here is what that means for you"
what: 1) Set-up, turn, punch line: three sentences, no weekday, no names that do not matter. 2) No clever bridge: say 'Here's what that means for you:'. 3) Finish the thought for the reader.
opening: I've been poor. And I've been rich. Rich is better.
who: John Carlton, direct-response copywriter (OHP golf, self-defence, health)
record: One-legged golfer ad: 'ran in the golf magazines for 15 years, and it's still running online'; still paying him royalties in 2026 (his page).
held_in: Taught as the shape of his selling stories; no own figure given on the page.
fails: Rambling detail; stories without the spelled-out meaning: adults absorb and move on.
why_he_says: It is the writer's job to complete the thought.
for_client: Baker: 'I baked with cheap flour. I baked with good flour. My neighbour only knocked once.' Then: 'Here is what that means for your breakfast.'
source: John Carlton, Telling Riveting Stories

method: Take the opening from the best salesman's live pitch
what: 1) Let the client's top salesman sell to you as if you were a real prospect (two hours, unaware if possible). 2) Write down his first sentences and the order. 3) Open the letter or film with them.
who: Drayton Bird, direct marketer (ex Ogilvy & Mather Direct vice-chairman, sold his agency to Ogilvy)
record: Letter to lawyers and follow-ups 'over £1,500,000 in sales'; launch letter for the Institute of Direct Marketing 'over 70% response' (his word).
held_in: Two pieces (mail and door-drop) 'based almost entirely on a 2-hour pitch'; client up 30% in three months (he says other factors too); another letter opening from a salesman's pitch 'still unbeaten in tests after 6 years'.
when: Anything sold by people: kitchens, cars, machines.
fails: not said
why_he_says: His bread depends on that pitch; nothing could be more powerful.
for_client: Kitchen showroom: film the first 20 seconds the oldest salesman says to a couple walking in; that is the ad's opening.
source: Drayton Bird, 51 Helpful Marketing Ideas, vol. 1
doubt: The 30% is not attributed only to it.

method: Say the limit first, from the authority
what: 1) Take the awkward legal or factual limit you must print anyway. 2) Move it from the small print to the first line. 3) Put the authority in front: 'Doctors agree: you can't ... without ...'.
opening: Doctors agree: you can’t lose weight without having a calorie-controlled diet.
who: Drayton Bird, direct marketer (ex Ogilvy & Mather Direct vice-chairman, sold his agency to Ogilvy)
record: Letter to lawyers and follow-ups 'over £1,500,000 in sales'; launch letter for the Institute of Direct Marketing 'over 70% response' (his word).
held_in: Slimming product ads after the law changed: 'the ads did just as well or better'.
when: Products with a compulsory warning or a known drawback.
fails: not said
why_he_says: Most people do not believe in miracles; admitted shortcomings make the rest believed.
for_client: Whitening clinic: 'Dentists agree: no gel whitens a crown.' First picture: one white crown among natural teeth.
source: Drayton Bird, 51 Helpful Marketing Ideas, vol. 1
doubt: "I believe"; no figure.

method: The trade name alone as first words
what: 1) Know one true thing about the reader from your list (his trade). 2) Begin with it, however plain: 'As an accountant ...'. 3) Say only what is true for that trade after it.
opening: As an accountant...
who: Drayton Bird, direct marketer (ex Ogilvy & Mather Direct vice-chairman, sold his agency to Ogilvy)
record: Letter to lawyers and follow-ups 'over £1,500,000 in sales'; launch letter for the Institute of Direct Marketing 'over 70% response' (his word).
held_in: 'I have seen exactly those words increase response by 200%' in a mailing (product: business loans).
fails: Data people and writers not talking to each other.
why_he_says: Something you know about your customer may matter more than anything about your product.
for_client: Laundry for salons: first words on screen 'As a hairdresser', first picture a tower of wet towels.
source: Drayton Bird, 51 Helpful Marketing Ideas, vol. 1
doubt: The proving mailing sold loans (excluded sector): only the method is taken.

method: Make the ad look like a write-up
what: 1) Set the ad in the paper's own editorial style, with the label 'Advertisement' kept. 2) Headline like a report. 3) Test against the ad-looking one.
who: Drayton Bird, direct marketer (ex Ogilvy & Mather Direct vice-chairman, sold his agency to Ogilvy)
record: Letter to lawyers and follow-ups 'over £1,500,000 in sales'; launch letter for the Institute of Direct Marketing 'over 70% response' (his word).
held_in: Magnet stores: customers praised the 'good write ups'; 'Every time I have tested an editorial style ad, it has improved results, for everything from charities to washing machines, by up to 123%'.
fails: "That does not mean all should": test.
why_he_says: People do not like ads; fit the environment.
for_client: Bed shop: local-paper report 'We weighed a ten-year-old mattress on Mill Street' marked Advertisement.
source: Drayton Bird, 51 Helpful Marketing Ideas, vol. 1

method: Yes / No / Maybe at the start of the decision
what: 1) Give two or three visible choices (Yes, No, Maybe/send me a sample). 2) Make Yes look better. 3) In film or post: ask to choose between two plain answers in the first seconds.
who: Drayton Bird, direct marketer (ex Ogilvy & Mather Direct vice-chairman, sold his agency to Ogilvy)
record: Letter to lawyers and follow-ups 'over £1,500,000 in sales'; launch letter for the Institute of Direct Marketing 'over 70% response' (his word).
held_in: Reader's Digest (Victor Ross): more Noes and more Yeses; John Francis Tighe's Maybe sticker worked; 'In my experience, this is always the case', e-mail too.
fails: not said
why_he_says: A choice forces them off the fence.
for_client: Gym: e-mail with three buttons: 'Yes, Tuesday', 'No, not for me', 'Maybe, show me the room first'.
source: Drayton Bird, 51 Helpful Marketing Ideas, vol. 1

method: First picture must be the subject itself
what: 1) Cover the words; ask a stranger what is being sold from the first picture. 2) If he names another product, change the picture. 3) Put a caption/line under the picture.
who: Drayton Bird, direct marketer (ex Ogilvy & Mather Direct vice-chairman, sold his agency to Ogilvy)
record: Letter to lawyers and follow-ups 'over £1,500,000 in sales'; launch letter for the Institute of Direct Marketing 'over 70% response' (his word).
held_in: US research he cites (bubble-bath girl read as soap, was drink); claims headlines below pictures get 27% to 105% better response (from Andy Owen).
fails: Ingenious, sexy or irrelevant pictures.
why_he_says: People assume that whatever is in the picture is what is sold.
for_client: Intercom firm: no smiling model; first frame the cracked old doorbell button next to the new one.
source: Drayton Bird, 51 Helpful Marketing Ideas, vol. 1
doubt: Second-hand research without source.

method: Say aloud what they feel but may not say
what: 1) Ask the team: what do these buyers believe, feel, desire about the matter? 2) Find the forbidden sentence they think at work. 3) Put it into the headline after 'for any <trade> who has ever felt like ...'. 4) Then offer the plain thing.
opening: Important news for any IT professional who has ever felt like telling an end user “Go to hell.”
who: Robert W. Bly, direct-mail copywriter, author
record: Own controls for planners, filters and software (his word); beat a Day-Timer competitor's control by 50% (told by Shleyner). [the training firm's letter test, told by Bly in his DM News column]
held_in: Seminar 'Interpersonal Skills for IT Professionals' had done badly with its title as headline; the new letter 'pulled 6X more leads than the control'.
when: B2B, trades, carers, teachers: people with a daily irritation.
fails: The seminar's own title as headline.
why_he_says: It names the core buying complex: beliefs, feelings, desires.
for_client: Booking software for hairdressers: 'For every hairdresser who has smiled and said "no problem" to a no-show.' First picture: an empty chair at 10:15.
source: Robert W. Bly, DM News column (File DMNCOL31)

method: Raise the buried line
what: 1) Read the running ad or your own draft to the end. 2) Find the sentence in the middle that makes you sit up. 3) Cut everything before it; make it headline and lead.
who: Robert W. Bly, direct-mail copywriter, author
record: Own controls for planners, filters and software (his word); beat a Day-Timer competitor's control by 50% (told by Shleyner).
held_in: Jim Rutz 'used a similar method to beat controls'.
when: Any draft, any running ad of a client.
fails: Warm-up paragraphs: in 8 of 10 drafts the first paragraph can go.
why_he_says: The best line is seldom first.
for_client: Client's 60-second film: the line at 0:41 'this hinge has closed 200,000 times' becomes second one.
source: Robert W. Bly, DM News column (File DMNCOL31)
doubt: shelf none: way of finding; the same advice in Shleyner.

method: The date of his last purchase as the opening
what: 1) Split the list by what each person bought and when. 2) First line states his own thing's age and what that means: 'Your X is now 3 years old and ...'. 3) No general pitch.
opening: Your PDR is now 3 years old and woefully out of date.
who: Robert W. Bly, direct-mail copywriter, author
record: Own controls for planners, filters and software (his word); beat a Day-Timer competitor's control by 50% (told by Shleyner).
held_in: Physicians' Desk Reference 'beat a long-time control' with list-specific mailings.
when: Replaceable goods, reference works, service intervals.
fails: not said
why_he_says: Start with the list.
for_client: Boiler service: 'Your boiler on Hill Road was last opened on 14 March two years ago.'
source: Robert W. Bly, DM News column (File DMNCOL31)

method: Product as hero, no mood scene
what: 1) First picture: the product large against a plain ground. 2) Leave out the period scene and people. 3) Test against the mood picture.
picture: the watch alone, large, dramatic, plain background
who: Robert W. Bly, direct-mail copywriter, author
record: Own controls for planners, filters and software (his word); beat a Day-Timer competitor's control by 50% (told by Shleyner). [Will Stone, Hamilton Watch, quoted by Bly]
held_in: Hamilton Watch reproduction of a 1920s watch (Will Stone): straight product photo generated three times as many sales as the "roaring twenties" scene.
fails: The unusual creative picture that hides what is sold.
why_he_says: The visual must tell the point by itself.
for_client: Goldsmith: ring on slate, close, turning; the couple on the beach is left out.
source: Robert Bly, Ads That Sell (On Target Advertising)

method: Trouble as a checklist question with a number
what: 1) Name the hidden condition. 2) 'Do you recognise the seven early warning signs of ...?' 3) The answer list is the content; the booklet is the thing sold.
opening: Do you recognize the seven early warning signs of high blood pressure?
who: Robert W. Bly, direct-mail copywriter, author
record: Own controls for planners, filters and software (his word); beat a Day-Timer competitor's control by 50% (told by Shleyner). [Charles Inlander, People's Medical Society, quoted by Bly]
held_in: People's Medical Society: more than 20,000 copies of a $4.95 book in about 10 runs in Prevention over three years.
when: Right magazine, readers who already care.
fails: Wrong publication.
why_he_says: Right product for the right audience.
for_client: Roofer: 'Do you recognise the five early signs of a tired roof?' First picture: a moss line under a gutter.
source: Robert Bly, Ads That Sell

method: Two-part technical opening: trouble question, then the rejected cure
what: 1) Question that only the right engineer can answer yes. 2) Second question names the usual cure and why he turned it down. 3) Third line: your product 'may be the answer'.
opening: Do you have a potable water supply or waste stream that contains organic contaminants? And have you considered activated carbon as the ideal treatment, only to ultimately reject deep-bed carbon installations because of the cost?
who: Robert W. Bly, direct-mail copywriter, author
record: Own controls for planners, filters and software (his word); beat a Day-Timer competitor's control by 50% (told by Shleyner).
held_in: Envira-Plus filter precoats letter: pulled an 11% response.
fails: Too clever, unclear headlines.
why_he_says: Restating the problem says you understand the reader.
for_client: Parking-lot sealing firm to facility managers: 'Do your bays puddle? And did you turn down resurfacing because of the price?'
source: Robert Bly, seven steps for high-tech products

method: Hidden benefit: study the buyer, not the product
what: 1) Ask: if I had godlike power to give my buyer any result he wanted from this, what would it be? 2) Write that as the headline though the product does not contain the word. 3) In the body show truthfully how the product leads there. 4) Test against the obvious benefit.
opening: The Ultimate Tax Shelter
who: Ted Nicholas, self-publisher (How to Form Your Own Corporation Without a Lawyer)
record: 'To date I've sold over 2,000,000 copies of this book', about 120 full-page ads (his word).
held_in: Over 200,000 copies through a single ad, 'there is not a word in my book about tax shelters'.
when: Books, services, tools with a consequence people want more than the thing.
fails: If the path from product to wish is not honest.
why_he_says: The hidden benefit comes from studying the potential buyer.
for_client: Wardrobe maker: not storage: 'Ten quiet minutes every morning.' First picture: a hand finding a shirt in the dark.
source: Ted Nicholas, The Ultimate Headline Secret (AWAI, Oct 2010)

method: Counted reasons or ways in front of the big benefit
what: 1) Specific number. 2) 'ways to' or 'reasons why'. 3) Big benefit. 4) If he already knows two, say so and keep the third.
who: Ted Nicholas, self-publisher (How to Form Your Own Corporation Without a Lawyer)
record: 'To date I've sold over 2,000,000 copies of this book', about 120 full-page ads (his word).
held_in: His ads and letters (no figure on this page).
fails: not said
why_he_says: Curiosity: he cannot resist the list of ways.
for_client: Optician: 'Three reasons your new glasses still give you headaches. You know two.'
source: Ted Nicholas, The Power of Reason Why Headlines (AWAI, May 2010)

method: Open on his scepticism, not on a benefit
what: 1) Name the thing he already bought and that failed him. 2) Headline: 'Why <the usual remedy> don't work'. 3) Reason. 4) Then what is different.
opening: Why Billberry and Lutein Don’t Work
who: Clayton Makepeace, financial and health copywriter
record: Health & Healing launch: 'We sold between one and two million subscriptions in three years' (interview with Bencivenga).
held_in: Vision supplement promotion, shown by him as his example that plain benefit heads no longer work in his field.
when: 200th benefit headline of the day; buyers of rival cures.
fails: Bob McCarthy and others in the thread: do not generalise beyond mail-order health and newsletters.
why_he_says: A benefit head screams 'another ad' and brings 'Yeah, right'.
for_client: Mattress shop: 'Why a harder mattress did not help your back.' First picture: board sliding under a mattress.
source: Bob Bly blog, Benefit Headlines Don't Work (15 Mar 2006)
doubt: No figure; shape must not hide a health claim.

method: Steal the sentence from a stranger's review
what: 1) Ask: who is he, what does he want, what does he use today, where is that discussed? 2) Read 500 reviews of books or goods for the same trouble (two to three hours), not of your product. 3) Paste exact phrases under: what he wants, pain, fear. 4) One phrase will stand out: use it word for word as headline.
opening: If you think you need rehab, you do.
who: Joanna Wiebe, Copyhackers founder, web copywriter
record: Published A/B tests for clients: Beachway, Dressipi, SweatBlock, 30+ startups in 2013 (own site).
held_in: Beachway rehab page: over 400% more clicks than 'Your Addiction Ends Here', over 20% more leads on the next page; no later version beat it.
when: No customers to interview, shy subjects, new seller.
fails: Looking only for reviews of the identical product; summarising the words.
why_he_says: "Instead of writing your message, steal it": you are not your prospect.
for_client: Snoring-mask dentist: read reviews of ear plugs. Headline: 'My wife sleeps better than I do. In the other room.' First picture: one pillow on a couch.
source: Joanna Wiebe, Amazon review mining (Oct 2014)

method: One blank sentence put to visitors
what: 1) Ask on the page: 'I want a wallet that ______'. 2) Sort the answers by theme, count them. 3) From the biggest pile take the phrase that raises an eyebrow ('a smarter, better-looking version of Excel'). 4) Turn it into the headline with a light touch.
who: Joanna Wiebe, Copyhackers founder, web copywriter
record: Published A/B tests for clients: Beachway, Dressipi, SweatBlock, 30+ startups in 2013 (own site).
held_in: Her monthly plan for clients; the same page cites Beachway: 26% more leads.
fails: Choosing ho-hum phrases.
why_he_says: Visitors tell you; your job is to feed it back.
for_client: Shoe repairer asks at the counter 'I want shoes that ___'; the winner 'that forgive me for walking to work' opens the film.
source: Joanna Wiebe, Conversion copywriting hacks for 2014

method: Zoom in: the embarrassment as a thing you can see
what: 1) Take the summary word (sweat relief, embarrassment). 2) Ask what it looks like on a Tuesday: ruined silk, a wardrobe of dark clothes, dodged high-fives. 3) First words: one such scene plus the physical act of the product ('just the dab of a towelette'). 4) Replace a stop-pain phrase by a tangible gain ('wear what you want'). 5) A later test may open with the pain in a sufferer's words.
opening: It doesn’t even have to be hot out. My armpits are ALWAYS wet.
who: Joanna Wiebe, Copyhackers founder, web copywriter
record: Published A/B tests for clients: Beachway, Dressipi, SweatBlock, 30+ startups in 2013 (own site).
held_in: SweatBlock home page: 108% lift in revenue; her MicroConf slides: a version with a pain-filled top section beat the earlier winner by another 49%.
when: Everyday embarrassing trouble; e-commerce page; colder visitors.
fails: Authority name at the top did not help people not yet caring.
why_he_says: Vague copy cannot be pictured; specific copy can.
for_client: Shoe-odour spray: first picture a guest's socks stepping over a doorway; words: 'You take your shoes off last. You always have.'
source: Joanna Wiebe, SweatBlock (Jun 2016); MicroConf 2017 notes
doubt: Several changes at once; the 49% stands in a listener's notes.

method: The button says what he will have, in his own voice
what: 1) Replace the act (sign up) by the result in the first person ('Show me outfits I'll love'). 2) Change headline and button together: a new headline alone may move nothing.
opening: Show me outfits I’ll love
who: Joanna Wiebe, Copyhackers founder, web copywriter
record: Published A/B tests for clients: Beachway, Dressipi, SweatBlock, 30+ startups in 2013 (own site).
held_in: Dressipi: new headline alone under 15% and not significant; with the button changed from 'Sign up now' 123.9% more clicks at 100% confidence.
fails: Headline tests alone (Dressipi, VueScan: flat after 36 days).
why_he_says: Headlines do not operate in isolation.
for_client: Curtain shop: button 'Show me my window in linen'.
source: Joanna Wiebe, Buttons vs headlines (Sep 2014)

method: Dull exact name beats the clever line
what: 1) Write what it is, where, for whom, in the searcher's own words. 2) No pun, no brand promise. 3) Test it against the clever one.
opening: Group Training & Fitness at Your Local Gym
who: Michael Aagaard, landing-page tester (ContentVerve, Unbounce)
record: About 300 copy-related split tests in four years (his word); tests printed with figures.
held_in: Fitness World (Scandinavian gyms), paid-search page: sold 38.46% more memberships than 'You Work Out Smarter at Fitness World'.
when: People who are already searching for a solution; paid search, shop pages.
fails: "I have yet to see a creative headline beat a clear headline in an A/B test" (online).
why_he_says: Searchers are in research mode; a clear line confirms they are in the right place.
for_client: Language school ad page: 'Evening Spanish for beginners, Mill Street, Tuesdays' instead of 'Speak your dreams'.
source: Michael Aagaard, 5 Landing Page Headline Formulas Tested (Jul 2013)

method: Benefit first; loss second; question last (searching visitors)
what: 1) For a page reached by search, open with the clear gain. 2) Use loss only when he owns something definite he may lose (rankings, money). 3) Use a question only when the answer is a loud yes.
who: Michael Aagaard, landing-page tester (ContentVerve, Unbounce)
record: About 300 copy-related split tests in four years (his word); tests printed with figures.
held_in: Three sites in three languages, little over 50,000 visitors together: benefit best, loss second, question last (one of the three is a betting forum); loss won for a duplicate-content tool.
when: Landing pages; visitors with a need.
fails: Questions, loss lines that need decoding.
why_he_says: They look for answers, not more questions.
for_client: Lock shop page: 'Open your door in 30 minutes, fixed price' not 'Locked out again?'
source: Michael Aagaard, 5 Landing Page Headline Formulas Tested (Jul 2013)
doubt: One of the three tests is a betting site (excluded sector); contradicts letter writers' question openings for cold people.

method: Form headline begins with Get and says what comes
what: 1) Start drafting with 'Get ...'. 2) Say what the subscriber receives in bullets. 3) Never the act ('sign up'). 4) Keep the word 'spam' away from the form.
opening: We guarantee 100% privacy. Your information will not be shared.
who: Michael Aagaard, landing-page tester (ContentVerve, Unbounce)
record: About 300 copy-related split tests in four years (his word); tests printed with figures.
held_in: ContentVerve form: 83.75% more sign-ups after clarifying bullets; a privacy line with the word spam reduced sign-ups by 18.70%, the one above raised them 19.47% (betting forum).
fails: A value line that is not relevant (it lost 12.45%).
why_he_says: Say what is in it for the receiver.
for_client: Vet clinic: 'Get the two dates your puppy needs this month'.
source: Michael Aagaard, High-converting sign-up form copy
doubt: Privacy test was on a betting site.

method: The one post that asks for nothing
what: 1) First line about him, specific. 2) Give the useful thing. 3) Say outright that you are not asking for a call or anything. 4) Stop.
who: Harry Dry, Marketing Examples newsletter
record: Newsletter "Read by 130k" (his site); 1M+ e-mails at 49.89% open rate (his word).
held_in: Lizzy's cold mail: answers went from 5% to 25% after she stopped asking; the only one of 97 that month Dry answered.
fails: The "quick call" ask.
why_he_says: Not asking is what made him reply.
for_client: Sign maker to café owner: 'Your blackboard is readable from 4 metres. I measured it. Nothing to sell, photo attached.'
source: Harry Dry, Lizzy's email worked on me
doubt: Lizzy's own figure; no sample.

method: Title as a promise one can feel cheated of
what: 1) Write the title as a promise. 2) Test: would the viewer feel cheated if the video did not keep it? 3) Plain 'How to ...' beats the decorated one.
opening: How to Start a Speech
who: Harry Dry, Marketing Examples newsletter
record: Newsletter "Read by 130k" (his site); 1M+ e-mails at 49.89% open rate (his word).
held_in: Among compared videos the one with 18M views.
fails: Titles that promise nothing.
why_he_says: A good title makes a promise.
for_client: Carpenter: 'How to hang a door alone' not 'Door diaries 4'.
source: Harry Dry, One of these videos has 18M views
doubt: Compares others' videos; no account median.

method: Ridiculous labour for the first few
what: 1) A plain offer (50% off). 2) Turn it into a physical game: 'The first five people to click this button 500 times win'. 3) Real limit.
opening: The first five people to click this button 500 times win 50% off
who: Harry Dry, Marketing Examples newsletter
record: Newsletter "Read by 130k" (his site); 1M+ e-mails at 49.89% open rate (his word).
held_in: Feastables e-mail: two million clicks from one e-mail.
when: Known brand with a young list; goal click.
fails: not said
why_he_says: Scarcity, labour, ridiculousness, game.
for_client: Trampoline hall: 'First ten to send us a photo of 50 jumps counted in chalk get in free.'
source: Harry Dry, Two million clicks from one email
doubt: Figure second-hand; a star brand.

method: Same quiet sign every time instead of a juicy subject
what: 1) One small mark (emoji) and 'New: Case Study #052'. 2) Same every issue. 3) Only after the content has earned trust.
opening: New: 🍿 Case Study #052
who: Harry Dry, Marketing Examples newsletter
record: Newsletter "Read by 130k" (his site); 1M+ e-mails at 49.89% open rate (his word).
held_in: Growth Design: 60% open rate.
fails: Unknown sender.
why_he_says: 9 of 10 compete on juiciness, one on reputation.
for_client: Butcher's Friday mail: 'New: 🥩 Cut no. 31'.
source: Harry Dry, Growth Design's 60% open rate

method: Ugly on purpose: the note instead of the design
what: 1) Hand-write the line on a Post-it or phone note. 2) Photograph. 3) Make ten in an afternoon and test.
picture: a handwritten Post-it
who: Harry Dry, Marketing Examples newsletter
record: Newsletter "Read by 130k" (his site); 1M+ e-mails at 49.89% open rate (his word).
held_in: $50K return on a 'Post-it' (numbers from Barry Hott and Ash).
fails: not said
why_he_says: Less polished, more authentic, ten tests in an afternoon.
for_client: Bike repair: a Post-it on a bent wheel: 'This took 11 minutes.'
source: Harry Dry, Make Ugly Ads
doubt: Second-hand.
