method: Story of a person first; the tool is only how
what: 1) Ask: what is the coolest thing a person can do with it, without naming it? 2) First line is that person and deed. 3) Product only as the hand tool in the picture.
opening: Redesigning signs in New York without anyone asking me to
picture: a designer before an ugly New York shop sign
who: Harry Dry, Marketing Examples newsletter
record: Newsletter "Read by 130k" (his site); 1M+ e-mails at 49.89% open rate (his word).
held_in: Adobe TikTok: 4.2M views.
fails: Brand self-praise.
why_he_says: You are the guide, not the hero: story first, product second.
for_client: Paint shop: 'Day 3 repainting my grandmother's kitchen while she is at the market.'
source: Harry Dry, Adobe's Perfect TikTok
doubt: Not his own work; no account median.

method: Ten titles, wait a day, keep the one they remember
what: 1) Write ten titles. 2) Show friends, ignore opinions. 3) After 24 hours ask which one they remember. 4) Use it. For cold visitors let the title name the problem, for warm ones the solution.
who: Harry Dry, Marketing Examples newsletter
record: Newsletter "Read by 130k" (his site); 1M+ e-mails at 49.89% open rate (his word).
held_in: His way for pages (Annie Maguire warm, Zenbu cold as examples).
when: Any first line before money for a test.
fails: Fancy titles that say nothing.
why_he_says: Being memorable is more important than being likeable.
for_client: Café: ten lines on the board, ask regulars next morning.
source: Harry Dry, How to write a landing page title
doubt: shelf none: way of choosing.

method: Test the number itself
what: 1) Counted list as the title. 2) Test several true counts (17, 28, 32, 45). 3) Keep the winner; do not round.
opening: 32 Ways to Save Time & Money from the Pages of Good Housekeeping
who: Milt Pierce, direct-mail copywriter (told by Eddie Shleyner)
record: Good Housekeeping book promotion 'ran, unbeaten by any other copywriter, for 20 years'. [told to Bly and Hatch in a round table, printed by Shleyner]
held_in: Good Housekeeping booklet promotion, 1980s: 32 beat 28, 17 and 45; unbeaten 20 years.
fails: not said
why_he_says: He tested many; 32 was the most successful.
for_client: Laundry booklet: test '14', '21' and '33 stains and what takes them out'.
source: Eddie Shleyner, In copywriting, specifics sell (Apr 2020)

method: Turn the resolution into a measured daily gain
what: 1) Find the abstract resolve in the old line ('next week I am going to get organised'). 2) Replace it by a countable thing per day ('at least one more hour of productive time each day'). 3) Say it is inside, and guaranteed if it is.
opening: at least one more hour of productive time each day
who: Robert W. Bly, direct-mail copywriter (told by Eddie Shleyner)
record: 'Bob's copy beat the control by 50%' (Day-Timer competitor).
held_in: Planner maker's control beaten by 50%.
fails: Abstract promise.
why_he_says: A headline must make or imply a fairly big, specific promise; need not be outrageous.
for_client: Meal box: not 'eat better': 'forty minutes of your evening back, four nights a week'.
source: Eddie Shleyner, Which headline won? (Aug 2021)
doubt: The page prints both headlines as pictures; only the part in quotation marks was readable.

method: Delete the first sentence, start in the middle
what: 1) Strike the greeting, the weather, the warm-up. 2) Ask of each next sentence: does it catch, educate, entertain, give context or prove? 3) Begin at the first one that does; inside the action.
who: Eddie Shleyner, copywriter, VeryGoodCopy
record: 95K newsletter subscribers (his LinkedIn line).
held_in: His e-mails and articles; reprinted by Ragan.
fails: Sentences without one of these jobs.
why_he_says: In medias res throws the audience into the action.
for_client: Wedding baker's reel starts at: '...and then the van braked.' First picture: cake box door opening.
source: Eddie Shleyner, Kill that first sentence (May 2019)

method: Cross-out test
what: 1) Write the opening. 2) Cross out your name, put in the rival's. 3) If it still fits, throw it away and find a fact he cannot say.
who: Eddie Shleyner, copywriter, VeryGoodCopy
record: 95K newsletter subscribers (his LinkedIn line).
held_in: His editing rule; no figure.
when: Any first line of a shop with rivals.
fails: Ambiguous lines.
why_he_says: Say what the competition cannot say.
for_client: Car wash: 'We care for your car' fits everyone; 'we wash the wheels first, with water we filtered twice' does not.
source: Eddie Shleyner, LinkedIn
doubt: shelf none: test of a line; no result.

method: Open on the fear under the spoken objection
what: 1) Note what rivals fight about (price). 2) Interview, ask why again. 3) Find the deeper fear (will my life arrive in one piece). 4) Open with that and the proof of care; let the others shout price.
who: Talia Wolf, GetUplift (conversion optimisation)
record: PowerUp Toys +95% website sales; US moving company +14% (her cases).
held_in: One of the largest US moving companies: 14% more conversions against the price-led page.
when: Services with risk: moving, surgery, repairs, child care.
fails: Joining the price race.
why_he_says: Price is said aloud; the fear drives the decision.
for_client: Piano mover: first picture a child's height marks on a door frame being wrapped; words: 'You are not afraid of the price.'
source: Talia Wolf, LinkedIn

method: Short subject with his own number or name
what: 1) Own name, or 2) a three-word line, or 3) the exact figure of the result in it; test against the plain title.
opening: 3 Subject Lines That Boosted Open Rates by 17%
who: Chase Dimond, e-commerce e-mail marketer
record: "$200M+ in email attributable revenue" (his site).
held_in: His own list: 'I increased my open rates by 17% with these 5 subject line tests' (five together).
fails: Vague curiosity, false urgency erode trust.
why_he_says: The subject is the e-mail's best salesman.
for_client: Dog groomer: 'Max, 11 weeks' as a subject line.
source: Chase Dimond, LinkedIn (Jan 2025)
doubt: One figure over five tests, no sample, no split per line.

method: Let the object speak: if this could talk
what: 1) Ask for the thing itself and hold it, worn, in your hand. 2) Note what it makes you see (a time, a place, who held it before). 3) Throw out the collector's data. 4) First line: if this ... could talk, what stories would it tell? First picture: the scuffed object in a palm.
opening: If this coin could talk, what stories would it tell?
picture: a worn old silver dollar in a hand (what he describes holding)
who: Clayton Makepeace, financial and health copywriter
record: Health & Healing launch: 'between one and two million subscriptions in three years'; coin company 'from 3 million a month to 16 million a month in sales' in 12 months (his word).
held_in: Coin company newsletter flyers: 3 million a month to 16 million a month within a year by presenting coins as historical artifacts.
when: Old, handmade, heirloom, regional goods; buyers who buy for feeling.
fails: Mintages and melt data 'just puts me to sleep'.
why_he_says: Buyers want the emotional connection; value is the excuse they give their wives.
for_client: Antique dealer: worn bread board in hand; 'If this board could talk, it would ask who is at the table tonight.'
source: The Copywriter Club podcast with Clayton Makepeace

method: The thing he said to himself last night
what: 1) Finish the sentence: last night he sat upright in bed and said 'Oh my God, I need to ___'. 2) Open with exactly that blank. 3) If you cannot fill it, you do not know him yet.
who: Clayton Makepeace, financial and health copywriter
record: Health & Healing launch: 'between one and two million subscriptions in three years'; coin company 'from 3 million a month to 16 million a month in sales' in 12 months (his word).
held_in: Advice he gave his writer Carline Anglade-Cole; learned in his first (fund-raising) letter.
when: Cold prospects with a worry or a wish.
fails: Rules-only, left-brain copy.
why_he_says: An unfulfilled desire or unaddressed fear is causing him fits right now.
for_client: Tax helper for shops: first picture a phone lit at 02:14; words: 'The box of receipts.'
source: The Copywriter Club podcast with Clayton Makepeace

method: Live through the customer's bad hour, scene by scene, and open with it
what: 1) Close your eyes and be him from door to door (waiting room, dull magazines, doctor's two minutes, scribble, gone). 2) Write each feeling. 3) Choose the strongest the trade never mentions. 4) Open with that moment.
who: Clayton Makepeace, financial and health copywriter
record: Health & Healing launch: 'between one and two million subscriptions in three years'; coin company 'from 3 million a month to 16 million a month in sales' in 12 months (his word).
held_in: First Health & Healing promotion (biggest seller of his life).
fails: Writing from product facts.
why_he_says: The prospect speaks to you first.
for_client: Dentist film from the patient's eye: ceiling tile with a water stain; words: 'You have counted these dots before.'
source: Clayton Makepeace, 8 ways to spot dominant emotions (AWAI, Apr 2015)

method: Only the headline changed: two headlines on one body
what: 1) Finish the body. 2) Print two headlines. 3) Same list, same day. 4) Roll out.
who: Clayton Makepeace, financial and health copywriter
record: Health & Healing launch: 'between one and two million subscriptions in three years'; coin company 'from 3 million a month to 16 million a month in sales' in 12 months (his word).
held_in: Unnamed client package: second headline 13.9 orders against 9.8 per thousand, 'a 34% lift above my original headline'; new package beat the control (3.9) by more than three to one in ROI; 25-45% lifts seen often.
fails: Headlines are not told.
why_he_says: Nothing equals the headline in pushing response.
for_client: Same 20-second film of the bakery, two first lines, 100 € each.
source: Clayton Makepeace, Grab Your Prospect by the Eyeballs (AWAI, 2014)
doubt: shelf none: a testing method; wording not given; 34% on profit/ROI basis.

method: Start with a sentence he already believes, and bend it
what: 1) Write the statement your audience already holds true. 2) Let the second half draw a consequence he never drew ('for every illness there is a country where it does not exist'). 3) Then the proof.
opening: For every illness, there is a country where it simply doesn’t exist …
who: Clayton Makepeace, financial and health copywriter
record: Health & Healing launch: 'between one and two million subscriptions in three years'; coin company 'from 3 million a month to 16 million a month in sales' in 12 months (his word).
held_in: Given by him among winners of the trade (no figure beside this one).
fails: Pure benefit heads in crowded markets.
why_he_says: A proposition makes him nod and then tantalises.
for_client: Carpet shop: 'In every old hotel there is one corridor carpet that never wears out.' First picture: that corridor.
source: Clayton Makepeace, Grab Your Prospect by the Eyeballs (AWAI, 2014)
doubt: The example is a health claim: shape only.

method: Take the blame off him
what: 1) Name his guilt (started too late, let it go). 2) First lines hand the fault to somebody or something real. 3) Stand with him in the same boat. 4) Offer a small revenge or relief just for reading on.
opening: Not With My Life You Don’t
picture: photo of the editor with 'No more Mr. Nice Guy'
who: Clayton Makepeace, financial and health copywriter
record: Health & Healing launch: 'between one and two million subscriptions in three years'; coin company 'from 3 million a month to 16 million a month in sales' in 12 months (his word).
held_in: 'Retirement Wealth Builder' magalog for Phillips' Retirement Letter (a control of his; no figure on the page).
when: Goods people feel guilty about: debt-free saving, weight, teeth, learning.
fails: 'Retire RICH!' would lack credibility.
why_he_says: Turns passive guilt into active anger, removes the salesman-prospect stand-off.
for_client: Dentist for anxious people: 'It is not your fault you have not come for nine years. Somebody hurt you.'
source: Clayton Makepeace, Connecting with Your Prospects’ Dominant Emotions (Early to Rise, Aug 2015)
doubt: Retirement newsletter (investing); anger at politicians must not be taken over.

method: The outside carries a name that already has goodwill with him
what: 1) Ask who this exact group already likes and trusts (a colleague, a happy customer of their trade, a respected person). 2) With permission, put that name first, not yours. 3) A small note from him explains why.
who: Dan Kennedy, direct-response copywriter and consultant
record: Says results, no audited list; his letters are the trade's teaching standard.
held_in: Statue of Liberty restoration fund-raising: 'a big bump' by changing the envelope from the Statue to Lee Iacocca.
fails: Name without permission, or not known to them.
why_he_says: Recognition, reputation, respect, but above all goodwill.
for_client: Dental-software: a mail from a dentist in the next town, his face first: 'I asked them to let me write to you.'
source: Marketing Speak podcast 61, Getting Into the A-Pile with Dan Kennedy

method: His own thing, seen at once
what: 1) List what this person is proud to be (fly fisher, gardener, his trade). 2) Let the first picture be unmistakably that thing. 3) Business only after.
who: Dan Kennedy, direct-response copywriter and consultant
record: Says results, no audited list; his letters are the trade's teaching standard.
held_in: His mailing practice: such pieces are opened first.
fails: General look.
why_he_says: Specific relevance bars the door and opens yours first.
for_client: Garden-tool sharpener: first picture a split grafting knife on a thumb; words: 'For hands that know this knife.' Only gardeners stop.
source: Marketing Speak podcast 61, Getting Into the A-Pile with Dan Kennedy

method: Describe him to himself as the reason it came to him
what: 1) From the list or place you know his work and habits. 2) Open with three or four true sentences about his day. 3) End: that is why this is for you. 4) Every sentence must be truly known, not fished.
who: Dan Kennedy, direct-response copywriter and consultant
record: Says results, no audited list; his letters are the trade's teaching standard.
held_in: Built into his letters; "highly skilled copywriters tend to build this in".
fails: Vague lines that fit anybody are the fortune-teller's trick; do not use.
why_he_says: I know enough about you to describe you to you.
for_client: To hotel housekeepers' chiefs: 'You know which floor smells of chlorine. You have moved the same stain three times.'
source: Marketing Speak podcast 61, Getting Into the A-Pile with Dan Kennedy
doubt: He takes it from cold reading; only the truthful form may be used.

method: Underdog slot: they laughed until
what: 1) Who doubted the buyer? 2) 'They all laughed when I ... until I ...' with his own real deed. 3) One visible triumph.
opening: They all laughed when I sat down at the piano until I started to play
who: Dan Kennedy, direct-response copywriter and consultant
record: Says results, no audited list; his letters are the trade's teaching standard.
held_in: He calls it plug-in-anything reliable (after Caples).
fails: not said
why_he_says: People are underestimated and mocked, and then triumph.
for_client: Man learning to bake: wife's raised eyebrow; second five: empty plate.
source: Marketing Speak podcast 61, Getting Into the A-Pile with Dan Kennedy

method: Many doors: four best fascinations on the outside
what: 1) Read the whole product; write dozens of one-line teasers, each with its page number. 2) Choose the four that touch four different everyday fears. 3) Put only these on the envelope, thumbnail set or first seconds. 4) The page number proves it is there.
opening: How to make your car very, very hard to steal
who: Mel Martin, Boardroom copywriter (told by Brian Kurtz, Boardroom executive)
record: Book of Secrets: over 20 million mailed, over half a million sold, after the same book had flopped twice under other titles.
held_in: Book of Secrets, Boardroom: from 'one of the biggest losers' to 'one of our biggest winners'; one mailing of 9 million.
when: Products with much content; mixed audiences.
fails: Titles that name the work (Book of Checklists) or the abstraction (Great Book of Inside Knowledge: worse).
why_he_says: Multiple entry points on universal concerns capture a very large audience.
for_client: Hardware shop reel: four half-second shots with four lines: 'the screw never to use in plaster' ... aisle number on each.
source: Brian Kurtz, The Master of Fascinations

method: Bloodhound: someone who finds out for you who cheats you
what: 1) The speaker is no guru, he is the one who goes and finds out. 2) First line names an institution and what it does not say ('what credit companies don't tell you'). 3) Show the source.
opening: What credit companies don’t tell you
who: Mel Martin, Boardroom copywriter (told by Brian Kurtz, Boardroom executive)
record: Book of Secrets: over 20 million mailed, over half a million sold, after the same book had flopped twice under other titles.
held_in: Boardroom packages for decades.
when: Consumer know-how; publications, shops with expertise.
fails: Promises the page does not keep: buyers telephoned to check every page number.
why_he_says: A truth seeker on your behalf makes the copy "vibrate".
for_client: Optician: 'What the chain shop does not write on your lens receipt.' First picture: magnified receipt.
source: Brian Kurtz, The Master of Fascinations

method: But / therefore instead of and then
what: 1) Write the opening story in beats. 2) Between every two beats put 'but' or 'therefore'. 3) Where only 'and then' fits, cut.
who: John Forde, copywriter, Great Leads co-author
record: Agora controls (his field); no figure on the page.
held_in: Taken from the makers of a long-running weekly TV series; used in his sales stories.
fails: "And then" beats lose the viewer.
why_he_says: Every beat must force or turn the next.
for_client: Boiler man: 'The baby was due Friday. But the boiler died Thursday. Therefore I drove with no socks.'
source: John Forde, A Surprising Storytelling Secret (Copywriter's Roundtable)
doubt: No result of his own.

method: Serial e-mails: each subject opens what the last left open
what: 1) Plan mails as episodes of one true story. 2) End each before the turn. 3) The next subject names the open thing. 4) The product stands inside the story as what was used.
who: Andre Chaperon, e-mail writer (Autoresponder Madness)
record: Says his whole business runs on e-mail sequences; no figure.
held_in: His own list business; the host claims double to quadruple response.
fails: Stories told without knowing the reader's pain; "most people don't do it right".
why_he_says: Readers come to expect something good when the name appears.
for_client: House builder: seven mails on one difficult roof; subject 3: 'the beam came back from the saw'.
source: Email Marketing Podcast 6 with Andre Chaperon (Drop Dead Copy)
doubt: No measured result.

method: Prizes and gifts that are the product's own world, with one joke prize
what: 1) List what only your world can give (dinner with the mayor, your own park bench). 2) Put them as short 'What have you won?' questions. 3) Last prize is a wink at the rival world (one-way ticket out).
opening: What have you won? A week at the Plaza? An evening with Mayor Lindsay at Gracie Mansion telling him how to run the city? ... Your own park bench?
who: Bill Jayme, direct-mail copywriter (told in his "20 Opinionated Answers")
record: Launch packages of New York Magazine, Mother Jones, Bon Appetit, Smithsonian, Food and Wine; "Do you close the bathroom door" envelope.
held_in: Launch of New York Magazine.
fails: Hawaii trip or camper prizes fit everybody.
why_he_says: Prizes should reflect the product.
for_client: Bakery opening: 'What have you won? The first loaf out on Sunday? Your name on a roll? One minute alone with the oven door open?' No lottery where law or faith forbids: a thank-you draw without stake or a straight gift.
source: Denny Hatch blog 89, Found: A Lost Treasure by Bill Jayme (Apr 2020)
doubt: A sweepstakes; for us only as a gift list without stake.

method: Break the line in the middle of the sentence at the fold
what: 1) End the first screen, slide or page inside a sentence. 2) The cut-off word must be the one he wants. 3) Continue at once on the next.
opening: They then began to remove their (continued on next page)
who: Bill Jayme, direct-mail copywriter (told in his "20 Opinionated Answers")
record: Launch packages of New York Magazine, Mother Jones, Bon Appetit, Smithsonian, Food and Wine; "Do you close the bathroom door" envelope.
held_in: His rule for carrying the reader to page two.
fails: Ending page one with the paragraph.
why_he_says: To carry the reader over.
for_client: Tile setter carousel slide 1: 'When we lifted the last tile we found a child's'
source: Denny Hatch blog 89, Found: A Lost Treasure by Bill Jayme (Apr 2020)

method: The outside is only a window: stop, look, listen
what: 1) Treat the envelope, cover, thumbnail as shop window. 2) Talk up to the reader, never down. 3) Money saved in money, not percent ('Half off!' at most). 4) Photograph rather than drawing.
who: Bill Jayme, direct-mail copywriter (told in his "20 Opinionated Answers")
record: Launch packages of New York Magazine, Mother Jones, Bon Appetit, Smithsonian, Food and Wine; "Do you close the bathroom door" envelope.
held_in: His packages for dozens of magazine launches.
fails: Puns that mislead ("pizzazz": people thought pizzas).
why_he_says: People open what interests them, not a format.
for_client: Upholsterer: cover says '84 euro less than a new seat, same frame', photo of the worn seat.
source: Denny Hatch blog 89, Found: A Lost Treasure by Bill Jayme (Apr 2020)

method: A neighbour's scrawl
what: 1) Handwritten notice, hurried, one small smiley. 2) 'We are working in your neighbourhood'. 3) Short words, the named local manager signs in the same hand. 4) Local phone number.
picture: plain sheet that looks scrawled by hand, smiley at point four
who: Denny Hatch, keeper of the Who's Mailing What! archive
record: Watched about 1,800 mailings a month for 30 years; counts "Grand Controls" (mailed three years or more).
held_in: Andersen Windows Philadelphia inserts: kept coming in the Sunday paper week after week ('successful ... I keep receiving it').
fails: Handwriting that does not match the signature.
why_he_says: People buy from people; ugly works.
for_client: Gutter cleaner: note photographed on a windscreen: 'We are on your street Thursday. Murat.'
source: Denny Hatch blog 191, Andersen Windows (Jun 2023)
doubt: Success inferred from repetition.

method: Let the reader in on how you came to him, and make it a compliment
what: 1) Say the awkward truth: you are on a list, this is not your first such letter. 2) Say what that list says about you, kindly. 3) Say less than you know ('dumb down what you know').
opening: If the list upon which I found your name is any indication, this is not the first -- nor will it be the last -- subscription letter you receive.
who: Denny Hatch, keeper of the Who's Mailing What! archive
record: Watched about 1,800 mailings a month for 30 years; counts "Grand Controls" (mailed three years or more).
held_in: Newsweek, Ed McLean: control many years, tens of millions; Axel Andersson counted 1,127 letters: 42% pinned to flattery.
fails: Reeling off private facts is creepy.
why_he_says: Make prospects feel good about themselves and they respond.
for_client: Furniture film targeted to new home owners: 'You are seeing this because you bought a house and did not buy a sofa the same day. Good.'
source: Denny Hatch blog 107, Flattery (Sep 2020)

method: Real paper, real signature, one to one
what: 1) Nothing sells on the outside. 2) Feel and look of a letter from one person (stamps, weight, blue ink). 3) First line to him alone. 4) In film: one person, one lens, no captions first second.
picture: closed envelope with embossed silver card, two real stamps, no teaser
who: Denny Hatch, keeper of the Who's Mailing What! archive
record: Watched about 1,800 mailings a month for 30 years; counts "Grand Controls" (mailed three years or more).
held_in: American Express Platinum launch: mailed over two years; about a quarter-million members at $250 a year (his estimate); National Trust version pulls up to 20% better.
fails: Computer signature fonts.
why_he_says: The signature is your salesman's handshake.
for_client: Tailor to 40 old customers: card with a cloth swatch and one written line.
source: Denny Hatch blog 190, Disbelief (Jun 2023)
doubt: A charge card (credit): only the letter form is taken.

method: A customer's letter to you as the whole headline
what: 1) Read the drawer of letters. 2) Take one that begs or confesses, in his words. 3) Print it as the headline, quoted. 4) The sales letter answers it.
opening: Dr. Hittich, my father and grandfather both died of heart attacks before age 50. And I'm age 48, and I'm scared to death
who: Ted Nicholas, self-publisher
record: Sold 2,000,000+ copies of one book; started with a fudge shop $96,000 in debt (his word).
held_in: Green Power (Netherlands): multimillion-dollar campaign.
when: Health, family, repairs: products people write about.
fails: Letters left in drawers.
why_he_says: It does not sound like a headline; no agency would write it.
for_client: Piano teacher: 'My mother is 71 and wants to play one song at my wedding. Can you help?' First picture: the note.
source: Ted Nicholas interview, IncomeDiary

method: Loss before gain
what: 1) Write gain and loss headline. 2) Name the owned things one by one (home, cash, car). 3) Test.
opening: How to avoid losing your home, your cash, your cars ... in a lawsuit?
who: Ted Nicholas, self-publisher
record: Sold 2,000,000+ copies of one book; started with a fudge shop $96,000 in debt (his word).
held_in: Information products: millions of dollars; loss "out-pulled" hope over the years.
when: Cold print and mail readers who own something.
fails: Contradicted on search pages by Aagaard (benefit first, loss second).
why_he_says: Fear of loss attracts more readers than hope of reward.
for_client: Roofer: 'How not to lose a ceiling, a carpet and a Sunday to one tile.'
source: Ted Nicholas interview, IncomeDiary

method: Show the making at the roadside
what: 1) Take the process out of the back room to where people pass. 2) Do it large, by hand (copper kettle, steam). 3) Sign says 'see ... made' and 'free samples'. 4) Change the words on the sign and count stops.
picture: a big copper kettle of fudge stirred outside the shop
who: Ted Nicholas, self-publisher
record: Sold 2,000,000+ copies of one book; started with a fudge shop $96,000 in debt (his word).
held_in: Peterson's House of Fudge: 25,000 cars a day, three bankrupt before him; a traffic jam after the outdoor kettle; words like "free samples", "see candy made" changed how many stopped.
when: Food, crafts, workshops; film of the same.
fails: A shop nobody stops at.
why_he_says: People wanted to know what was going on.
for_client: Noodle shop: hand-pulling at the window 12:00-13:00, sign 'see lunch made'; reel opens on the pull.
source: Ted Nicholas interview, IncomeDiary
doubt: His own staging used a briefly dressed woman (not taken); only the making is.

method: Read to page 117: the headline is a sentence inside the thing
what: 1) Read the whole product with 3x5 cards. 2) Note each fact that surprises. 3) Write up to 250 headlines. 4) Make it true and seeming true: add who says so in the line under it.
who: Ted Nicholas, self-publisher
record: Sold 2,000,000+ copies of one book; started with a fudge shop $96,000 in debt (his word).
held_in: Bill Fisher's failed book retitled and re-headlined from page 117 (cancer claim, not to be used).
fails: True but unbelievable headlines.
why_he_says: The headline is some 73% of success.
for_client: Cookbook: page 88 'onions first in water' becomes the film's first line.
source: Ted Nicholas interview, IncomeDiary
doubt: The proving headline is an unacceptable health claim; 73% has no source.

method: When the great ones need it, here is what they do
what: 1) Take out the sale from the headline. 2) Name three buyers everybody knows. 3) 'When A, B and C need ..., here's what they do ...' 4) Page answers.
opening: When eBay, Disney, and Marriott need SEO help, here’s what they do…
who: Conversion Rate Experts (Karl Blanks, Ben Jesson)
record: Moz: 52% more sales in a split test, 5,000+ visitors; Crazy Egg 363% growth (own case pages).
held_in: Moz PRO page: 52% more sales than the old page ('Improve your traffic and rankings with an SEOmoz PRO Membership!').
fails: Rushing into the sale in the headline.
why_he_says: A headline is to make visitors stop and pay attention, not to sell.
for_client: Stair builder: 'When three embassies had a creaking stair, this is what they asked for.' (with permission)
source: Conversion Rate Experts, Moz case study
doubt: Whole page changed.

method: The customer who refuses tells you the next opening
what: 1) In the last offer ask: if you decide not to take it, reply in one line why. 2) Count the reasons. 3) The commonest becomes the first thing said next time.
opening: IF YOU DECIDE YOU DON’T WANT TO CLAIM THIS SPECIAL $1 OFFER … then please send a reply to this email with a brief explanation of why you aren’t interested.
who: Conversion Rate Experts (Karl Blanks, Ben Jesson)
record: Moz: 52% more sales in a split test, 5,000+ visitors; Crazy Egg 363% growth (own case pages).
held_in: Moz e-mails; part of the four months that added $1 million a year.
fails: Guessing objections.
why_he_says: How do you read minds? Ask.
for_client: Dance school after a trial week: 'If you are not coming back, tell me why in one line.' The line opens the next reel.
source: Conversion Rate Experts, Moz case study

method: Opposite idea
what: 1) Write what everybody in the trade tells people to do. 2) Say the reverse where you can prove it. 3) Keep it about the reader's relief ('had enough of being told').
who: David Deutsch, Boardroom copywriter
record: One of four writers "responsible for over 650 million pieces of successful direct mail" at Boardroom (Kurtz).
held_in: A health promotion: 'had enough with all these people telling you all those things not to do ... It got your attention.'
fails: Reversal without proof.
why_he_says: If everyone zigs, zag.
for_client: Garden shop: 'Stop raking. Your lawn eats leaves.' First picture: mower over leaves.
source: The Copywriter Club podcast 415, Copythinking with David Deutsch (2024)

method: Twenty headlines on twenty different guesses about him
what: 1) Each headline must stand on another hypothesis of what he wants (money, pride, teacher proved wrong, trip). 2) Not word variants. 3) The headline sells reading the next line only.
opening: how to prove wrong your sixth grade teacher who said you'd never amount to anything
who: David Deutsch, Boardroom copywriter
record: One of four writers "responsible for over 650 million pieces of successful direct mail" at Boardroom (Kurtz).
held_in: His practice and teaching; no figure.
fails: Trying to make the headline a sales pitch.
why_he_says: Maybe your guess of the wish is wrong.
for_client: For a gym: shame, staircase, grandchild, suit, doctor, sleep: six films, six first lines.
source: The Copywriter Club podcast 415, Copythinking with David Deutsch (2024)
doubt: shelf none: way of working; transcript wording rough.

method: A report among look-alike boxes
what: 1) Look at the page or feed where all rivals stand. 2) Make yours look like a short news item, not a box. 3) Headline: 'Don't call any X until you read this' or the pain + 'read this before ...'. 4) News, a solution, something free, all true.
opening: WARNING: Don't Call Any Chiropractor Until You Read This Announcement!
who: Gary Halbert, direct-mail copywriter, The Gary Halbert Letter (1986-2007)
record: Family-crest letter: 7,300,000 cash-with-order customers (his figure).
held_in: His yellow-pages advice (invented sample); same shape "WARNING: Don't Hire Any Interior Decorator Until You Hear This" ran for Kacey Furniture (Denver, +40% in six weeks).
when: Directories, search results, local feeds; buyer ready, undecided whom.
fails: Copy that does not deliver the promised information.
why_he_says: People are far more likely to read what appears editorial; here they look for a solution.
for_client: Locksmith map post: 'Before you call any locksmith, ask this one thing: the price of the cylinder.'
source: The Gary Halbert Letter, "Yellow pages"
doubt: Sample claims in the letter are invented by him: shape only; carry the ad label.

method: The professional's confession
what: 1) Give the license first. 2) 'Here is my secret:' 3) The one thing of his trade he has never done or never buys. 4) 'Why? The answer is simple.'
opening: I Have Never Filled A Prescription In My Life!
